Git & GitHub

A saved file, a local commit and a successful push are three different milestones.

IN THIS CHAPTER

01Check readiness before tapping Push02Make the remote deliberately03Review a local snapshot04Prove that the remote received it05A small branch experiment06Try it yourself07Common mistakes

All 19 chapters →

What you will learn

  • Prepare Git, clone or initialize, review changes and push truthfully.
  • Keep credentials out of source and understand branches.

Before you begin

Git installed, your own repository, network for remote operations. Practice in a disposable repository, not important shared work.

Check readiness before tapping Push

Source Control can show INSTALL GIT and Initialize repository when those prerequisites are missing. Credentials now live in the panel’s ⋮ → Git Credentials; use a token with the needed repository Contents read/write scope. Do not paste credentials into this course, a terminal URL or a source file.

A local commit does not require a remote. Push requires a reachable remote and appropriate credentials. A token that can push may still lack permission to create a GitHub repository.

Make the remote deliberately

  1. On GitHub, create a disposable repository under your account; choose private unless you intend public sharing. Initialize it with a README if you want a first branch to clone.
  2. Copy its HTTPS repository URL. In CodeC use Projects → + → Clone Git Repo, supply the URL and a project name, then open it in the Editor.
  3. For an existing local project, initialize it if necessary. Create the repository on GitHub first, then use Source Control’s Remotes dialog to add its URL, normally named origin.

This manual-first flow avoids assuming repo-create rights. The source-supported Publish flow defaults private where offered; review its visibility and token needs before using it.

Review a local snapshot

  1. Edit README.md with one harmless line and wait for autosave. Open Source Control and inspect the diff.
  2. Stage only the intended source files. Check that no token, private note or generated binary is included.
  3. Write a meaningful commit message. Use the available commit action; COMMIT & PUSH may create a local commit before a remote attempt. Read both outcomes.

Unresolved conflicts are grouped and block the commit. Read both versions, resolve the file, then Mark Resolved; do not use that button to pretend a conflict is understood.

Prove that the remote received it

Read the result’s repository/remote/branch. “Committed locally — NOT pushed” is not success on GitHub. An unpushed ↑N indicator means local commits still need publication. A first push can establish upstream; a failed push keeps the local commit safe for a PUSH retry.

Open the intended repository and branch on GitHub to verify the changed file. Do not solve a rejected push by force-pushing over work you have not reviewed. Fetch/pull and inspect the history or conflict first.

A small branch experiment

Switch Branch lists local/remote branches and a New branch action. CodeC can stash dirty work and restore it when returning, but that is not a substitute for a backup. In a disposable repository, create a practice branch, change a line, commit and push it, then return to the original branch and compare.

For a local terminal experiment after committing clean work, the following uses only your disposable repository. Replace the original-branch placeholder with the branch name you recorded; do not paste angle brackets literally.

Observe state before a branch change

git status
git branch --show-current
git log -1 --oneline

Expected: a clean status, your current branch and the latest local commit. These commands do not prove a push; remote verification is separate.

Try it yourself

  1. Make and push one README change; verify the exact file on GitHub. Expected: local and remote agree.
  2. Commit another change while offline. Expected: a local commit can exist, but remote publication must wait; reconnect and retry deliberately.
  3. Create a disposable branch and compare its file with the original branch. Expected: branch-specific versions, not lost work.

Common mistakes

  • Commit is not upload. Read the push result and correct branch.
  • Never store a token in the repository or a screenshot.
  • Ignored artifacts are not source backups; the user’s .gitignore is respected.
